cases.question: Based on our pace and what's left, should we ask the client for more doors, or a second pass on the turf we have?

facts.name: doors we can knock in the days left

answer.question: Based on our pace and what's left, should we ask the client for more doors, or a second pass on the turf we have?
answer.answer:
To determine whether to ask the client for more doors or to conduct a second pass on the current turf, we need to compare the projected capacity (based on the last 7 days' average daily doors multiplied by the number of days left) with the number of untouched doors remaining in the current turf. If the projected capacity is greater than the untouched doors, it is advisable to ask the client for more doors first [doc:program-plan#more-doors-or-a-second-pass]. If the untouched doors exceed the projected capacity, a second pass on the not-home doors is the fallback option [doc:program-plan#more-doors-or-a-second-pass].

A door is counted once per day, regardless of how many times it is knocked on that day [doc:counting-doors#doors]. An attempt is every knock record the canvassing app submits. If a canvasser knocks a not-home door at 11:00 and comes back at 14:00, that is two attempts and one door [doc:counting-doors#attempts]. A second pass on a not-home door adds a door on the day of the second pass [doc:counting-doors#doors].

If the untouched doors exceed the projected capacity, it is recommended to continue working on the current turf. A new office should sit closest to the doors we still need: the untouched doors in our turf, weighted by how many doors each precinct has left [doc:program-plan#opening-another-office]. Untouched or lightly touched precincts (under 25 percent of doors touched) that are dense (over 2,000 doors per square mile) are worth a new office; sparse precincts (under 1,000 doors per square mile) are slow to knock and are better handled at the end with drive-out shifts [doc:program-plan#opening-another-office]. Candidate sites are listed in the candidate office sites table [doc:program-plan#opening-another-office].

In that case ask the client for more doors first; new turf contacts voters at the normal first-pass rate. A second pass on not-home doors is the fallback, because second passes contact voters at roughly half the first-pass rate. If untouched doors exceed capacity, keep working the turf we have.

A door is one address unit (a house, or one apartment unit) knocked on one day. Our dashboard counts each door once per day no matter how many times it was knocked that day. Doors knocked on different days count again on each day, so a second pass on a not-home door adds a door on the day of the second pass.

cases.question: Why does the client's daily report show more doors than our dashboard for Oct 12?

answer.question: Why does the client's daily report show more doors than our dashboard for Oct 12?
answer.answer:
The client's daily report shows more doors than our dashboard because it counts attempts (including repeat attempts and those later rolled back), while our dashboard counts doors once per day with rollbacks removed. The gap between the two is typically due to repeat attempts or rollbacks. 

- The client's report includes all attempts before QC rollbacks [doc:counting-doors#why-the-client-s-numbers-differ-from-ours].
- Our dashboard removes rollbacks and counts each door only once per day [doc:counting-doors#why-the-client-s-numbers-differ-from-ours].

args.query: client daily report vs our doors

sources.text: The client daily report counts attempts, pulled at the end of each day before any QC rollback. Our dashboard counts doors with rollbacks removed. The gap on any day is the repeat attempts at the same door plus any attempts that were later rolled back. A normal day shows a gap of a few percent from repeat attempts. A larger gap almost always means a rollback.

cases.question: What counts as flash knocking under our QC rules?

answer.question: What counts as flash knocking under our QC rules?
answer.answer:
Flash knocking under our QC rules is recording doors faster than a person can walk to them and knock. A shift is flagged when 10 or more consecutive knocks are recorded less than 30 seconds apart. Confirmed flash knocking is rolled back: the knocks in the window no longer count as doors or contacts. A whole shift recorded this way is rolled back in full.
- Definition: Recording doors faster than a person can walk to them and knock [doc:qc-rules#flash-knocking]
- Flagging threshold: 10 or more consecutive knocks less than 30 seconds apart [doc:qc-rules#flash-knocking]
- Consequence: Confirmed flash knocking is rolled back [doc:qc-rules#flash-knocking]

answer.question: What counts as flash knocking under our QC rules?
answer.answer:
Flash knocking under our QC rules is recording doors faster than a person can walk to them and knock. A shift is flagged when 10 or more consecutive knocks are recorded less than 30 seconds apart. Confirmed flash knocking is rolled back: the knocks in the window no longer count as doors or contacts. A whole shift recorded this way is rolled back in full.
- Definition: Recording doors faster than a person can walk to them and knock [doc:qc-rules#flash-knocking]
- Flagging threshold: 10 or more consecutive knocks less than 30 seconds apart [doc:qc-rules#flash-knocking]
- Consequence: Confirmed flash knocking is rolled back [doc:qc-rules#flash-knocking]
